items.quote: How the True Physick, which is covered bark and rind, is to be got out, and rightly prepared by Fire
items.note: The chapter heading names its subject: getting the True Physick out of what covers it and preparing it by Fire.

items.quote: which is covered bark and rind
items.note: The heading says the True Physick is covered, as by bark and rind; it has to be got out.

items.quote: ALL things in respect of the first matter were created perfect, but the Chymist perfecteth the last matter by Fire
items.note: Croll sets first matter (created perfect) against last matter (perfected by the Chymist through Fire).

items.quote: The Physitian perfecteth the Creature of God by Fire.
items.note: The margin note gives to the Physitian what the paragraph gives to the Chymist, perfecting by Fire.

items.quote: nothing in this lower world (which is subject to generation and corruption) is so noble but hath Poyson in it selfe
items.note: Every thing of the lower world holds poison, and the Physick lies very near it.

items.quote: where there is hurt there is also help, where there is venome there is vertue
items.note: Hurt and help, venom and virtue stand in the same place in God's works.

items.quote: which the sublunary Elements bring forth, should alwayes be joyned together in all things, to put us dayly in mind of the Fear of God
items.note: Good and evil are joined in all things by Nature's order, as a reminder of the Fear of God.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: A writing named beside the passage on good and evil joined together.

items.quote: As soon as the Omnipotent gave Power to Man, presently he raised up an enemy, least the Power growing lazy should loose its Nature
items.name: Firmianus
items.note: Words given to Firmianus: an enemy was raised up against man's power so that it would not grow lazy.

items.quote: nothing is in every respect happy
items.name: the Poet
items.note: A saying given to an unnamed Poet; the margin gives a Latin form of it.

items.quote: Nil ex omni propte
items.name: the Poet
items.note: The margin note gives the Latin of the Poet's saying; part of it is unreadable in the transcription.

items.quote: that man partaker of the Divine Nature, and Lord of all living creatures, should be vexed with Ghosts, and hurryed with Furies
items.note: Man, though partaker of the Divine Nature, is vexed; the text continues the theme of an enemy set beside power.

items.quote: in the same place or thing where of his MERCY he appoynted plenty of Physick, even there also by the power of his incomprehensible Justice he substituted Poyson to guard it
items.name: Roger Bacon
items.note: Words given to Roger Bacon: where God set Physick by mercy, he set Poison by justice to guard it.

items.quote: he substituted Poyson to guard it
items.note: The Physick is guarded by the poison set in the same thing; it is not freely open.

items.quote: Thistles and prickles of Roses the inseperable companions and avengers of transgressions
items.note: Thistles and the prickles of roses stand as figures for the guarding poison joined to the good.

items.quote: Good cannot be known but by evill, and the Enemy being discovered the danger may be avoyded
items.note: Good is known through evil; the text does not show whether this sentence is still Bacon's or Croll's own.

items.quote: The severe Justice of God is the disease & venome in all things: on the contrary, the Mercy of God is the Physick in Nature and in all things.
items.note: The margin note says what Justice and Mercy stand for here: disease and venom on the one side, Physick on the other.

items.name: Wisd.; Eccl.
items.note: Writings named beside the Bacon passage.

items.quote: Holy Hermes the most Ancient Divine (together with Ecclesiasticus) writeth in his Key that all sublunary things ought to consist of contraposition and contrariety
items.name: Hermes; Ecclesiasticus
items.note: Hermes in his Key, with Ecclesiasticus, is given the view that sublunary things consist of contrariety.

items.quote: writeth in his Key
items.note: A writing of Hermes is named by its title, the Key.

items.quote: this after another manner may be of things Impossible in respect of the generation and corruption of things
items.note: An obscure clause: the contrariety may hold after another manner of things Impossible; the lines given do not explain it.

items.quote: All things that are awlesse are also lawlesse
items.note: Croll joins being without awe and being without law.

items.quote: nor can Man any other way attaine to the highest pitch unlesse he resolve constantly to maintaine the good fight that is finished in faelicity
items.note: Contrariety calls man to a constant fight, ending in felicity.

items.quote: God by his Wisdome hath ordained that Sympathy and Antipathy should be alike good
items.note: Sympathy and Antipathy are both called good by God's order.

items.quote: he would stir up mortall men to contemplate and search out his secrets
items.note: God's secrets in Nature are there to be searched out; the spectacle of Nature is meant to stir men to it.

items.quote: Heraclitus called Nature the daughter of War
items.name: Heraclitus
items.note: Heraclitus is cited for Nature as born of war.

items.quote: Homer called it Contention
items.name: Homer
items.note: Homer is cited for Nature as Contention.

items.quote: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy.
items.what: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy
items.note: The margin heads the paragraph as giving the cause of Sympathy and Antipathy.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Writings named beside the Sympathy and Antipathy passage.

items.quote: Man is his own enemy
items.note: The cause of dissolution and death lies within man himself.

items.quote: in it lyeth hid the preserver and destroyer of health
items.note: Both what preserves and what destroys health lie hidden in the body, the little world.

items.quote: the Saints have called the mortall body Hell and Purgatory, wherein continuall war is to be made
items.name: the Saints
items.note: The Saints are cited as naming the body Hell and Purgatory.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: A writing named beside the passage on the body's inner war.

items.quote: Nature hath commanded the Physitians to be ministers, and to seperate, not masters to compose
items.note: The physician's work is to separate as Nature's minister, not to compound as master.

items.quote: our Remedies require preparations, separations and exaltations before they can impart their hidden and restrained vertues
items.note: Three steps named for remedies: preparation, separation, exaltation; only then do their virtues act.

items.quote: their hidden and restrained vertues
items.note: The virtues of remedies are hidden and held back until the work frees them.

items.quote: the Tryall of the knowledge of Physick is to be made by Fire: Physick and Chymistry cannot be separated
items.note: Physick is tried by Fire and is joined with Chymistry.

items.quote: not that which Mountebanks use to paint Faces with to make them White and Red
items.note: The text sets its Chymistry apart from the face-painting of mountebanks.

items.quote: doth make manifest, not onely the true Simples, Wonders, Secrets, Mysteries, Vertues, Forces respecting health
items.note: Chymistry makes manifest what is secret and mysterious in things.

items.quote: the Archaeon Ventricle or Naturall In-bred Chymist
items.note: The text glosses the Archaeon Ventricle as the natural in-bred Chymist, which art imitates.

items.quote: it teacheth to segregate every mystery into into its own reservacle
items.note: Each mystery is set apart into its own receptacle.

items.quote: to free the medicines from those scurvy raggs wherein they were wrapt up by a due separation from the impurities and corruptible and filthy mixture of superficiall and externall Elements
items.note: Medicines are freed by separation from the impure outer mixture that wraps them.

items.quote: that pure and Christiline matter may be administred to our bodies
items.note: The result of the separation is named as a pure, crystalline matter given to the body.

items.quote: But to deliver this from prison and captivity
items.note: The medicine is spoken of as a prisoner to be delivered; with the rags and wrapping this is figure, not plain speech.

items.quote: Hoc opus, hic labor est
items.name: UNCLEAR
items.note: A Latin saying is quoted and Englished as a hard task; the text names no source.

items.quote: without this Chymicall Phylosophy all Physick is but livelesse; Without Alchymicall skill there can be no Speculative or Practick Physick
items.note: Croll makes Chymical Philosophy and Alchymical skill the condition of all Physick.

items.quote: He that rejecteth that knowledge being disheartned by the difficulty thereof shall never find where the disease lyeth
items.note: Whoever gives up the difficult knowledge will not find where disease lies.

items.quote: our common sort of Physitians are not to be followed, who patronize their sloth under other mens paines and study
items.note: Croll rejects the common physicians who leave preparation to careless apothecaries.

items.quote: I speake not against the conscientious Apothecaries who by their trusty diligence serve the Common Wealth as the Alchymy of Vulcan
items.note: Conscientious apothecaries are excepted and likened to the Alchymy of Vulcan.

items.quote: By this artificall resolution of bodyes the propertyes which before layd in the compositions of them are now brought to light
items.note: Resolving bodies by art brings to light properties that lay within their composition.

items.quote: as by a certaine kinde of artificiall Tynosure, or figures of stars
items.note: The art is likened to a guiding star or figures of stars by which the Chymists find their way through Nature.

items.quote: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies (as hath been said)
items.note: The text points back to an earlier place where this analysis was spoken of.

items.quote: there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found either in the Salt, or Mercury, or Sulphur of the same body
items.note: Every constant quality of a body lies in its Salt, Mercury or Sulphur.

items.quote: all compound bodies of the inferiour Globe are to be distributed into three orders or companies; into Animalls, Vegetables, and Mineralls
items.note: A first step of the work: bodies are sorted into three orders before examination.

items.quote: the three First things (viz. Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury)
items.note: Salt, Sulphur and Mercury are named together as the three First things.

items.quote: For in the shop of Nature there is Animall, Vegetable, Minerall Salt; Animall, vegetable, minerall Sulphur; vegetable, animall, minerall Mercury
items.note: Each of the three First things occurs in each of the three orders.

items.quote: Vegetables comprehend plants, trees, Zoophyts. Animalls are the beasts in their order, creeping swimming, flying, four footed creatures.
items.note: The margin note says what Vegetables and Animalls include.

items.quote: The first face of Things was pure, sound, perfect without corruption and death
items.note: Things were first made pure and incorrupt.

items.quote: Man at first was created healthy, (sicknesse entred by the Woman, not by the Man)
items.note: Sickness came in by the Woman, as the text states.

items.quote: there appeared two contraries, the externall corruptable, and the internall compleat, which could not long continue in one without unavoydable corruption
items.note: Death enters through two contraries, outer corruptible and inner complete, joined in one.

items.quote: the transgression and fall from unity to alterity
items.note: The Fall is named as a fall from unity to alterity.

items.quote: by the curse of God new Tinctures came in (even infinite evills)
items.note: The text glosses the new Tinctures as infinite evils.

items.quote: the beauty of the whole Creature was transplanted
items.note: The Creature is said to be transplanted; the margin note explains the word.

items.quote: The transplantation of the Creature is by the calamity and coming in of sicknesse upon it
items.note: The margin says what the transplantation of the Creature means: sickness coming upon it.

items.quote: since the Fall me carry in their own bosome their enemy both of creation and propagation, which causeth sicknesse and death by in-bred contrariety and corruption
items.note: Since the Fall men carry their enemy within; the note echoes Man is his own enemy in CH3.6.

items.quote: Impurity was joyned to the pure roots, which was the predestination of diseases
items.note: Diseases arise from impurity joined to pure roots.

items.quote: the roots of sicknesses in certaine individuall or species doe not consist apart by themselves, but are implanted and mixt in the pure and first seeds of things
items.note: Roots of sickness are mixed into the pure seeds of things, not apart from them.

items.quote: the foure wombs or Elements
items.note: The Elements are named as four wombs in which seeds spring up.

items.quote: Nature therefore, as it is now, gives us nothing that is pure in the world, but hath mixed all things with many impurities
items.note: Nothing pure is given now; all is mixed with impurity.

items.quote: we should begin to learn the knowledge of Chymistry from our cradles
items.note: The mixture of impurity is a spur to learn Chymistry from childhood.

items.quote: we ought to till and manure the EARTH, to wit, the whole frame of the world
items.note: The text says the EARTH to be tilled means the whole frame of the world, not soil alone.

items.quote: both the Visible and Invisible (Limus) Earth
items.note: The text speaks of an Invisible Earth beside the visible, with the Latin word Limus set beside it.

items.quote: in this LAND of LABOUR to attain the fruits of Terrene and Caelestiall Wisdome
items.note: The world is named in capitals as the LAND of LABOUR; its fruits are earthly and heavenly wisdom.

items.quote: this is the true end of Mans Creation, that in the fear of God and love of his neighbor he should manage the Earth, recovering what he hath lost
items.note: Man's end is to manage the Earth and recover what was lost; the Earth here follows the sense given in CH3.12.

items.quote: he should continue the Instrument, Habitation and Tabernacle of God
items.note: Man is to remain God's instrument and dwelling.

items.quote: he should through Nature search out the wonderfull works of God by consideration of Temporall and Caelestiall observations, thereby to make known the invisible works of God
items.note: Searching Nature makes God's invisible works known.

items.quote: wonders and mysteries which he hath revealed
items.note: The mysteries spoken of are those God has revealed.

items.quote: He that hath learned to know God & himselfe hath ordered the Earth with good husbandry
items.note: The margin makes knowing God and oneself the good husbandry of the Earth, so tilling the Earth is not meant plainly.

items.quote: idlenesse the pillow & cushion of the Devill is removed by labour and diligence
items.note: The note sets labour against idleness, as in CH3.12.

items.quote: this Separatory art which teacheth rightly to discerne and seperate the Good from the Bad, the Profitable from the Unprofitable
items.note: The art is named by its work of separating good from bad.

items.quote: the Stupefactive from Fire, the minerall Spirit from the Anthos or blossome, the Homogeneans from the Heterogeneans, Poyson from healing Medicines and Balsoms
items.note: A list of separations the art makes.

items.quote: the Anthos or blossome
items.note: The text glosses Anthos as blossom.

items.quote: that which is pure Celestiall, the kernall and Marrow, from that which is Terrestrial Impure, the Rinds, and Membranes, the Covers, Shells, Husks and dreggs, the Coate aed Cottage of Physick
items.note: The pure part is covered by rinds, shells and husks; the same covering named in the chapter heading.

items.quote: the Soul the Inhabitant thereof, the Super-elementall mystery the Quint-Essence, which is the true Internall, sutable, freindly and correspondent Balsom of our bodyes
items.note: The text names the Soul of the Physick as the Quint-Essence and calls it the true inner Balsom of our bodies.

items.quote: whose faculty mounts more high and quick being loosed from its chaines
items.note: The quickening essence is spoken of as chained and loosed, like the prisoner of CH3.7.

items.quote: All Venemous things have a Balsom agreeable to Mans Nature, and there is no poysonous Creature but hath in it an Antidote against its own poyson
items.note: Every poison holds its own antidote and balsom.

items.quote: Spiders are good for hens and Sparrowes, Toads for Serpents, Serpents for Staggs and Storks
items.note: Examples that what is poison to man is food to another creature.

items.quote: these Formes of Physick work better when they are extracted, then whilst they are drowned in Matter, which alwayes hindereth and restraineth the power and operation of the Secret
items.note: Extracted Forms work better; Matter restrains the Secret.

items.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
items.note: The margin makes putrefaction the only true corrective of Physick.

items.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
items.note: The note says putrefactions only are the true correctives; CH3.20 says poison is corrected and amended by the Art and Fire. The note goes on to give Fire the separating work, so the two may describe different steps.

items.quote: As Death separateth eternall and perishing things, so doth Fire the good from the bad, the Quint-Essence from the body.
items.note: Fire separates the Quint-Essence from the body as Death separates the eternal from the perishing.

items.quote: Even the Soule or Form of every kind of thing
items.note: The text joins Soule and Form as one.

items.quote: hath not onely more, but more excellent vertues and operations by far than either the very body, or the matter of the same thing
items.note: The Form has more and better virtues than the body or matter.

items.quote: by how much the more it hath of the Form, by so much the more is there of the Entity
items.note: Being grows with the share of Form.

items.quote: the very Enemyes of Chymistry are forced to confess
items.name: the very Enemyes of Chymistry
items.note: The opponents of Chymistry are said to confess this by ocular demonstration.

items.quote: Hence many advantages follow.
items.note: Announces a numbered list of advantages (First, Secondly, Thirdly).

items.quote: Reasons why the Spagyrick Physick duely prepared is to be preferd before other Hetroclite mixtures in the shops.
items.note: The margin heads the list as reasons for Spagyrick Physick over the shops' mixtures.

items.quote: First, Because many sick people will take it more easily and willingly
items.note: First advantage: the sick take it more willingly than muddy potions.

items.quote: the Physitian himselfe that prescribed it, and the Apothecary that mingled, would abhor and altogether refuse to drink in the like case
items.note: The common potions are such that their makers would refuse them.

items.quote: Secondly, Though these medicines be often used, yet they hurt not the stomack
items.note: Second advantage: no harm to the stomach.

items.quote: they are by a naturall force carryed without hinderance to their known lodgings
items.note: Separated medicines go of themselves to their places in the body.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because all the hurtfull quality is altogether cast out of, or at least easily kept under in these Essences
items.note: Third advantage: harm is cast out or kept under in the Essences.

items.quote: this Spagyrick art is so necessary that he can be no safe Physitian who hath it not
items.note: No physician is safe without the Spagyrick art.

items.quote: in one simple thinge there are different substances, somtimes of contrary qualityes, whereof one may be hurtfull, the rest healthfull
items.note: A simple holds contrary substances, known only by separation.

items.quote: the Galenists may make good their Axioms, who affirm that all bitter things are hot
items.name: the Galenists
items.note: The Galenists' axiom is reported and tested against opium, roses and succory.

items.quote: The knot of this Answer must be cut with an Anatomicall knife fire
items.note: The anatomical knife is fire: anatomy here means separation by fire, as in CH3.8.

items.quote: in Opium there is a sweet Narcotick Sulphur, and a bitter hot Salt penetrating by a subtile resolution and causing sweat without any stupefactive vertue
items.note: Separation shows opium as a sweet narcotic Sulphur and a bitter hot Salt.

items.quote: yet may it be so corrected and amended by the help of this Art and of Fire, that it may be taken into the whole body without danger
items.note: The poison of metals can be corrected by Art and Fire.

items.quote: who can tell how to pick and cull the best things out of the worst
items.note: Skilful physicians draw the best out of the worst.

items.quote: it is tamed artificially with Salt-Peter, by the assistance of Fire
items.note: An unruly poison is tamed with saltpetre and fire; the name of the substance is partly unreadable in the transcription.

items.quote: Poyson reduced to its Arcanum is not poyson, but a soveraign nedicine
items.note: The margin says poison brought to its Arcanum stops being poison.

items.quote: stinking smells by degestion are turned into sweet savours
items.note: Digestion turns stinking smells sweet.

items.quote: thus the earthy {G123: 1 letter illegible}lnets are healed of their Lepr{G124: 1 letter illegible}sie
items.note: Something earthy is healed of leprosy; the word is partly unreadable and is not guessed.

items.quote: Mineralls whose spirits exceed ours in subtilty, and precious stones, ought to be accounted medicinable, which rightly prepared doe much excell all Vegetables in effecting cures
items.note: Minerals and precious stones, rightly prepared, excel vegetables; a numbered list of reasons follows.

items.quote: Nor can it be that Vegetables which are obnoxious to corruption should so free Mans body from corruption, as the Spirits of perfect mettalls doe
items.note: First reason: what is incorruptible frees from corruption better.

items.quote: there being scarce any Oyntment prepared that is not made of an imperfect mettall or minerall
items.note: Second reason: surgery already uses imperfect metals, so perfect ones have more force.

items.quote: perfect things doubtlesse have received of the Omnipotent far greater force and vertues
items.note: Perfect things hold greater force.

items.quote: could by no means so contemper the mixture of those bodies that they should attaine to such admirable power and admit of the solid and stable Nature of a Balsom
items.note: Third reason: living things and plants cannot take the stable nature of a Balsom.

items.quote: Because stones require a long time of generation, but perfect bodies are generated in a shorter space
items.note: Fourth reason: length of generation gives stones a greater faculty.

items.quote: but perfect bodies are generated in a shorter space
items.note: CH3.25 ties greater faculty to a long time of generation and says perfect bodies are generated in a shorter space; CH3.23 gives perfect things far greater force. The lines given do not reconcile the two.

items.quote: in the Bohemian Garnat is such that it can hardly be spoyled or corrupted by any force of Fire, and that onely because of the fixation of spirits that may be seen in it
items.note: The Bohemian Garnet withstands fire by the fixation of spirits.

items.quote: may well be preferd before the Orientall Rubie in Physick, which can scarce indure the Fire as many hours as the other can months
items.note: Endurance in fire is the measure by which the garnet is preferred to the ruby.

items.quote: precious stones have the Colour, Forme and Tincture more or lesse from Mettalls by formation of the Stars, for they are transplanted Mertalls
items.note: Stones take their tincture from metals by the stars; they are transplanted metals.

items.quote: for they are transplanted Mertalls
items.note: Transplanted is used here of metals becoming stones, while CH3.11 and N169 use it of the Creature under sickness.

items.quote: Rubies and Garnats have the Tincture of Gold, Saphirs and Turcoides of Silver, Emeralds and Chrysolites of Copper, the Jacint and Topaz of Iron, the Diamond of Tinne
items.note: A table of stones and the metals whose tincture they carry.

items.quote: factitious and fictitious gemms that are made of the powder of red lead and white flints proportionably mixed, receiving a mettallick Forme from Fire
items.note: False gems are made from red lead and white flints by fire; offered as proof of the metal in stones.

items.quote: the skilfull Stone-gravers can easily discerne the cheat and fraud by their softnesse and lightnesse
items.note: Made gems are known by softness and lightness.

items.quote: Gemmes are Elementary Stars.
items.note: The margin names gems as Elementary Stars.
